extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, empirical researchers, and policymakers studying patent litigation outcomes
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis of how industry, technology, procedural posture, district, and plaintiff/defendant characteristics affect patent-litigation outcomes (invalidity, infringement, summary judgment, trial, and appeals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-specific variation in patentee win rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcomes vary significantly by industry: patentees win a majority of cases in pharmaceutical (51.6%) and often in energy (40.0%), but fare poorly in biotechnology (8.3%), communications (14.8%), consumer goods and services (15.1%), and computer and electronics (17.1%). These differences are highly significant (p = 0.000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating patent litigation outcomes, account for industry as a major predictor; compare industry win rates (see Table 9 and Figure 6) and report statistical significance. Use industry-specific baselines rather than assuming uniform outcomes across all sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish technology area from industry of deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors distinguish the nature of the technology claimed from the industry in which the patent is deployed (e.g., biotechnology technology area vs biotechnology industry category; chemistry generally vs pharmaceutical chemistry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should avoid conflating technology taxonomy with industry categories because litigation incentives, regulatory context, and outcomes may depend on the industry in which the patent is exploited. Explicitly classify patents both by technology area and by industry of deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for invalidity differ across industries
rubrics_metrics.description: The prevalence and success rates of invalidity grounds differ significantly by industry: no significant difference for §102 prior art rulings; modest but significant differences for inadequate disclosure (§112); and highly significant differences for §103 (obviousness) and indefiniteness (p = 0.000 for obviousness differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing invalidity risk, break down which statutory grounds are being asserted and report industry-specific success rates (e.g., obviousness success ranges from 0% in some industries to 77.8% in construction). Do not treat invalidity as homogeneous across industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary-judgment success on invalidity varies by industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall, just over 30% of summary judgment motions on invalidity were granted; industry rates vary widely (e.g., energy industry had 0% success rate on invalidity SJs (0/17), while biotechnology had 56.3% success). Table 12 reports SJ invalidity frequencies and percentages (Pearson χ2(10) = 22.2267; p = 0.014).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate procedural-stage outcomes separately: summary-judgment rates on invalidity are industry-dependent. Analyses of early-case resolution should include industry-specific SJ grant rates and consider how local court practices (e.g., permission to file SJs) might affect these numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural posture matters but effects are uneven
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in outcomes are not driven uniformly by trial outcomes or summary judgments on noninfringement (those were not statistically significant), but summary-judgment rulings on invalidity exhibit significant industry differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report outcomes by procedural posture (summary judgment, trial, appeal) and test which stages drive observed industry or technology differences. Do not aggregate across stages without checking for heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue/district effects influence outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: District choice affects patentee win rates. In multivariate regressions, patents filed in the Eastern District of Texas remained significantly associated with higher overall patentee win rate (p < 0.01). Inclusion of district dummies can reduce significance of other variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for forum/district in regressions; include key district dummies (e.g., ED Tex, District of Delaware, ND Cal) where feasible, and consider local procedural norms (e.g., judges requiring permission before filing summary judgment) that may bias observed rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and representativeness caveats for litigated-case datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: The dataset includes only litigated patents that reached rulings on summary judgment, trial, or appeals; it comprises less than 10% of filed lawsuits in the study years and under 0.1% of all patents. Settlements are typically confidential, so outcomes in settled cases are unobservable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize findings from dispositive-rulings datasets to all patents without caution. Explicitly acknowledge selection bias (cases reaching judgment may differ systematically) and quantify coverage (percentage of filed suits and of all patents) when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmaceutical-specific litigation incentives (Hatch-Waxman and reverse payments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pharmaceutical litigation is governed by Hatch-Waxman rules and often involves branded manufacturers with FDA-granted monopolies pre-litigation. Branded firms sometimes use reverse-payment settlements (paying generics) and face different settlement incentives and stakes than in standard commercial litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing pharmaceutical patent cases, model Hatch-Waxman incentives, the prevalence and effect of reverse payments, and differences in plaintiff/defendant stakes; these features can change which challenges reach adjudication and bias outcome distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entity type effects (NPEs vs operating companies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-practicing entities (NPEs) are common in software cases and differ from practicing entities: fewer settlement options (no cross-licenses), generally only monetary relief (less likely to get injunctions), different reputational incentives, and potential resource asymmetries with large defendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include patent-owner entity status as a covariate; expect NPE cases to have different settlement dynamics and possibly different likelihoods of going to judgment. Be aware empirical evidence on NPE settlement rate differences is mixed; study designs should attempt to control for repeat-litigator effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-specific outcome patterns (software vs chemistry/pharma vs biotech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology correlates with outcomes: chemistry and pharmaceutical patents are significantly more likely to be valid and infringed (e.g., chemistry patents found obvious only 9.7% and indefinite 3.0% in this dataset), software/computer-electronics patents largely lose (often via noninfringement rather than invalidity), and biotechnology shows very high invalidity rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When predicting litigation risk or interpreting empirical results, separate analyses by technology class and report technology-specific rates of invalidation, noninfringement, obviousness, and indefiniteness. Consider doctrinal stability differences across technologies as an explanatory factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-and-economics selection expectations (Priest-Klein 50% rule and deviations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Priest-Klein theory predicts a 50% plaintiff win rate in tried cases; subsequent literature identifies factors (asymmetric stakes, costs, agency issues, risk preferences) that can cause deviations. The authors' data are inconsistent with the strong 50% Priest-Klein hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame empirical findings relative to selection-theory expectations: test whether observed win rates deviate from 50% and explore candidate explanatory factors (asymmetric stakes, costs, risk profiles, agency costs). Use these frameworks to generate selection stories for industry/technology differences.
